item.title: Why We Want the Unavailable
item.description:
Relationships

Why We Want the Unavailable

The psychology behind desire, distance, and fantasy.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • Availability introduces reality; unavailability preserves possibility.
  • Scarcity magnifies attraction by increasing personal investment.
  • Playing hard to get can increase attraction when used moderately.
  • Seduction thrives on ambiguity; imagination amplifies excitement.

Some of the most powerful romantic feelings arise not from what we experience, but from what we almost experience. Unavailable partners often ignite desire precisely because they leave room for imagination—and imagination can be more seductive than reality.

The Appeal of the Unavailable

“Love may have the longest arms, but it can still fall short of an embrace.” —Megan McCafferty

Why do people become captivated by someone they cannot have? Whether the person is married, geographically distant, or otherwise out of reach, unavailability often intensifies attraction rather than diminishing it. The paradox is that unavailable partners are frequently desired not because they are better suited to us, but because their distance invites idealization.

A familiar belief—“all the good ones are taken”—reflects the assumption that highly desirable people are already claimed by others. Winning the affection of such a person can feel like winning a difficult competition, boosting both self-esteem and the perceived value of the relationship.

It is helpful to distinguish between two forms of romantic unavailability: situational, such as being married or living far away, and emotional, rooted in difficulties with intimacy or commitment. This post focuses on situational unavailability, where external circumstances, not emotional limitations, prevent the relationship.

Scarcity plays a central role. When something valuable is difficult to obtain, we naturally assign it greater worth. Scarcity rarely creates attraction on its own. Rather, it magnifies an attraction that already exists, making it feel more urgent and emotionally significant. The effort we invest in pursuing someone becomes evidence, in our own minds, that the goal must be worthwhile.

Source: Anna Pou/Pexels

When Imagination Takes Over

“It is our imagination that is responsible for love, not the other person.” —Marcel Proust

Unavailability does more than heighten desire—it expands imagination. Limited access leaves gaps, and we fill those gaps with our own hopes and assumptions. Psychologists call this positive projection: attributing desirable qualities to someone precisely because we do not know them well enough to see their imperfections. The halo effect amplifies this tendency. One appealing trait—beauty, confidence, intelligence, or mystery—can become the foundation for imagining an entire constellation of virtues. Because the unavailable person cannot easily disconfirm these assumptions, fantasy remains remarkably durable.

article continues after advertisement

Our fantasies extend beyond the other person. We also imagine a different version of ourselves, more attractive, more alive, more fulfilled. In this sense, unavailable partners entice us not only with who they appear to be, but with who we imagine we might become alongside them. Availability introduces reality; unavailability preserves possibility.

Why “Hard to Get” Works

“All really great lovers are articulate, and verbal seduction is the surest road to actual seduction.” —Marya Mannes

Two familiar romantic behaviors illustrate the psychology of unavailability: playing hard to get and seduction.

Playing hard to get leverages scarcity. When romantic access requires patience and effort, attraction often increases. As the sayings go, “the more you pay, the more it’s worth,” and “easy come, easy go.” Both sayings capture an important psychological principle: Effort increases perceived value, making relationships that require investment seem more precious. Indeed, research suggests that people value potential partners more highly when winning them requires effort, partly because personal investment increases perceived worth (Birnbaum et al., 2020).

Seduction similarly relies on partial access. As Robert Greene (2001) argues, effective seducers maintain a degree of ambiguity, delaying gratification while revealing themselves gradually. The excitement comes not from complete fulfillment but from anticipation. Imagination fills the remaining gaps, often making the fantasy more compelling than reality.

article continues after advertisement

Moderate idealization can benefit long-term relationships by encouraging partners to focus more on strengths than weaknesses. But excessive idealization carries risks: When fantasy replaces reality, disappointment becomes almost inevitable.

Why Unfinished Love Lingers

“Only unfulfilled love can be romantic.” —Maria Elena in Vicky Cristina Barcelona

Incomplete romantic experiences—a flirtation that never developed, an unresolved attraction, an affair that ended too soon, or lingering feelings for an ex—often remain emotionally vivid precisely because they never reached closure. As I have argued elsewhere, change, more than stability, generates emotion (Ben-Ze’ev, 2000, 2019). The experiences that occupy our thoughts most persistently are often those that never reached a satisfying conclusion (Ongchoco, 2026).

Unfinished experiences linger because the story remains open. Imagination continues writing new chapters. An unavailable partner becomes an emotional gap: impossible to fully possess, yet equally impossible to forget. For this to happen, the relationship needs an emotional beginning, enough momentum to awaken genuine hope, and an ending before resolution becomes possible. When these elements converge, the combination of desire, imagination, and absence can be extraordinarily powerful.

Concluding Remarks

“Absence sharpens love, presence strengthens it.” —Thomas Fuller

Some romances endure not because they were fulfilled, but because they were never allowed to become fully real. Unavailability magnifies desire, idealization perfects the beloved, and incompleteness keeps the story alive. The loves that remain unfinished often occupy more space in our hearts than those that run their natural course, suggesting that what we long for sometimes shapes us more profoundly than what we actually attain.

item.title: Could "Roster Dating" Be Right for You?
item.description:
Mating

Could "Roster Dating" Be Right for You?

Consider the possible risks and rewards of rostering in the dating market.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • "Roster dating" is when you date multiple people simultaneously without choosing one to date exclusively.
  • It can help if you don't want to date anyone exclusively or tend to jump into exclusivity too quickly.
  • However, it can be difficult to coordinate, delay decision-making, be a turn-off, and prevent depth.
  • If you choose to roster date, enforce limits and be honest and upfront with yourself and others.
Source: Paul Coartney/Shutterstcok

Are you currently dating three, four, seven, 10, or maybe even 42 different people? If so, you may be doing what's been dubbed on social media as "roster dating" or "rostering." That's when you keep dating multiple people simultaneously without choosing one to date exclusively. Maintaining such a lineup or roster of people to date for a while or even indefinitely could be a way of keeping your options open. But at the same time, it could be lining you up for some significant risks, especially if you do want to eventually go exclusive with the one who is the right fit for you.

Roster Dating Could Be for You if You Don't Want Exclusivity

Here's an exclusive: not everyone wants exclusivity. Maybe you'd just like to keep getting different things—such as sex, companionship, money, free meals, variety, and did I mention sex?—from different people on your roster. This could be your way of having your cake and eating it too—and going out to shows with it, and cuddling with it. You get the picture.

Roster Dating Could Help You Choose Among Dating Prospects

What if you are actually interested in having a committed relationship? Then roster dating for a little while could in theory give you more time to evaluate each of the possibilities and compare them with each other. This could be particularly useful if you don't really know what you want and need to experience different possibilities.

All of this could genuinely help if you tend to jump into exclusive relationships way too quickly—long before you even get to know what all of the different possibilities may be. When you are hungry, maybe the first hot dog stand that you see is not the best one to visit. Roster dating could be your way of entering a food court. Moreover, the best fit for you might not necessarily jump to the top of your lineup at the very start. People can take different amounts of time to warm up to you and show their true personalities.

Roster Dating Could Make You Less Desperate

Roster dating could in theory help guard against the D-word: desperation. When you aren't putting all of your eggs in one basket, and instead feel like you have more options, you may end up being more relaxed and confident on each of your dates. After all, if one does not work out, there's always the rest of the lineup, right?

article continues after advertisement

Roster Dating Requires Coordination and Extra Effort

In practice, though, you probably don't have a human resources department, TV production crew, or coaching staff to coordinate all the dates with all the different members of your roster. Thus, rostering could be confusing, complicated, and exhausting, making it difficult to keep everyone's story straight and remember details like each person's interests, background, and name.

Roster Dating Could Delay Decision-Making and Waste Time and Effort

All of that time and effort spent could be a big waste if you are roster dating for the wrong reasons. Sure, more time helps you to get more information. But do you really need more info about someone, for example, who already has shown more red flags than Christian Grey from Fifty Shades? Keeping around people who are definitely not going to be keepers will end up wasting your time and effort and theirs. So make sure that you aren't roster dating simply to delay or avoid decision-making.

Roster Dating Can Keep You From Getting Deeper With Anyone

Additionally, rather than providing you with enough information to best decide whom to go gaga over, roster dating could leave everything quite shallow with everyone. It's like any type of multi-tasking: Dividing your attention so much can prevent you from going deeper with any particular person or thing.

article continues after advertisement

Roster Dating Can Turn People Off

Here's another thing that could go wrong: People may drop off your roster as soon as they find out that you are roster dating. There's a reason why people don't typically recommend listing roster dating as one of your hobbies on a dating profile; the practice can lead to people feeling disrespected and used, especially when you don't take extra care to properly communicate your intentions. People may feel like you are somehow trying to create competition for your heart à la a reality TV dating show. That may turn off those who have other things going on in their lives—leaving you with a roster of only those who are more desperate.

If You Roster Date, Do It Carefully

Roster dating may or may not be for you, but if you do try it, take the following steps to avoid ending up causing or experiencing hurt:

  1. Enforce strict limits. This includes limits to the number of people you can handle at a time—typically, no more than four—and the length of time you date someone before making a final decision about him or her.
  2. Be direct and honest with others. While you don't have to start each date saying something like, "Hello, Number Five," it's good to be clear about not being exclusive yet and about your reasons why.
  3. Be direct and honest with yourself. At the same time, know why you are doing the roster thing, and make sure it's not for the wrong reasons

What you do can affect not only you but also those you attract. After considering the potential risks and rewards, you may decide to put roster dating on your roster of dating approaches. Or you may be opt for the one-by-one approach instead.

item.title: What You Need to Know About Donor Siblings
item.description:
Family Dynamics

What You Need to Know About Donor Siblings

Openness about donor siblings is key for you and your child.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • Many parents-to-be worry about the likelihood that their child will have multiple donor siblings.
  • Donor counseling may lead to fewer donations but is no guarantee that donors will limit offspring.
  • Early disclosure and up-to-date information is essential for all involved.
Source: prostoole / Magnific

The news is full of stories about donor-conceived children unknowingly dating in high school or feeling overwhelmed about the number of donor siblings they have. Some banks and agencies have made efforts to limit donations by each donor and educate donors about the long-term implications of donating to many families, which may incentivize donors to limit their donations. Some have even established communication systems with other banks to limit their donors’ donations.

However, stories like the one reported on CNN about the woman who inadvertently dated her “half-brother” in high school or the story about donor Jonathan Jacob Meijer, in the Netflix film The Man With 1000 Kids, have drawn a great deal of attention. It makes sense to feel paralyzed by these stories. But as I describe in my Zoom Out theory, this is precisely the moment to pause, review the facts, and focus on what you can do for your future family.

The questions for many recipients of egg or sperm donation are: Will it hurt my child to have many donor siblings, and is it possible to track donors?

The stress that many recipients carry can be heavy. Some even wonder if they should relinquish their long-held dream of having a child. They fear ruining their child’s life by bringing a child into the world with the potential for so many siblings. While it is true that there are people who have found it stressful, to varying degrees, to have many donor siblings, the research shows that donor-conceived children are thriving. It is important to note that early disclosure appears to be key in the development of a stable identity and solid relationship with the parents.

It is true that because donating sperm is much easier than donating eggs, children conceived with the assistance of egg donation may have fewer donor siblings. That said, it is still possible to have more than you may expect. Let’s consider the ways this can happen. Donors can donate to egg donation programs, egg banks, and clinics. They may also donate to friends or family members. A young donor may create many eggs, which may be more than a couple needs to complete their family. Therefore, there are possibly several children in each family, as well as many excess embryos frozen in storage.

It can be very difficult for parents to decide what to do with excess embryos, so sometimes, they are stored and used after decades. It has been estimated that there are over a million embryos stored, which can be used at any time. In fact, in the past year, we have seen healthy births from embryos that were two and three decades old. This means that with donated eggs or sperm, your child may have multiple siblings from each donation, resulting in donor siblings close in age to your child and other donor siblings the same age as your grandchildren.

article continues after advertisement

The subject of The Man with 1000 Kids lived in Denmark, a country that is small and attempts to limit the number of times each donor can donate. Even with these guidelines, this donor was able to donate to many clinics around the world and to many people individually. The U.S. is a much larger country with fewer guidelines and no country-wide legal regulations. Although charges were brought against Mr. Meijer, the country of Denmark was not able to control him.

Could we invent donor tracking software or fingerprint donors? Should we follow up with parents to document how many children they have created with donor gametes, or limit how long parents can keep their embryos frozen? Many ideas have been suggested, and the State of Colorado has enacted a law that attempts to address many of the issues that recipients are concerned about when using donor conception, including donor limits. As of January 1, 2025, Colorado has limited the donations in their state to 25 per donor. This law was a large step in the world of donor conception, but it is only one state and cannot account for some of the issues addressed here, such as donating privately or using excess embryos. So, the question becomes, what can we do?

Counseling donors may help. When I assisted in the creation of the first open donor program on the East Coast, I learned how helpful it was for many donors to be educated about the implications of their donation and even connect with their recipients. I found that the more the donor understood that they would likely be asked to respond to children created with their gametes, update families with medical information, and understand the meaning their donation had for these families, the more they seemed inclined to donate to fewer families. More donors are being educated, and more attention has been brought into the zeitgeist about this issue, yet even thoughtful counseling is not a guarantee that your donor will not donate to more people than you expect.

article continues after advertisement

The best thing you can do for your child is talk to them early and often about their origins and, over time, help them understand that having many donor-related siblings is a possibility. They may be in the same math class or sports team as a donor-conceived sibling. So, if your child is interested in dating someone who was also created with the assistance of donor conception, or whose parent was a donor, it may make sense to use a commercial DNA test to ensure they are not siblings. This may bother some children and not others, just like we see that some children love having many donor siblings and others do not. It is impossible to know how your child will react. Research shows that early disclosure is connected to a more stable identity and a stronger relationship with you. Some children will find this information completely unremarkable, some will feel good about it, and others may have more to process. Either way, the foundation of openness you build will be one of the greatest gifts you will give them.

item.title: On Narcissism and Romantic Relationships
item.description:
Narcissism

On Narcissism and Romantic Relationships

Old narcissistic injuries can undermine the capacity for intimacy.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • Neurotic narcissism undermines many intimate relationships.
  • The narcissist's grandiose persona defends against feelings of inferiority and unlovability.
  • Romantic relationships can trigger buried narcissistic rage from early emotional injuries.
"Narcissus," attributed to Frans de Neve
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain

A common occurrence in psychotherapy is seeing a patient who seems unable to form any lasting or satisfying long-term romantic relationships. Frequently, they tend to be attracted to emotionally or otherwise unavailable individuals, resulting in repeated failed attempts to establish intimate bonds. In some cases, these same or similar dynamics can be observed in patients who are already in a committed but problematic, volatile, unstable, and stormy relationship. Everyone knows that good communication is essential for healthy relationships. But what happens when clearly communicating just isn’t enough? This is something psychotherapists see frequently: couples having serious difficulties for which teaching them basic communication skills is simply not sufficient. What’s going on in such cases?

Freud once remarked that in the marriage bed, there are at least six people present. He referred, of course, to the respective parents. And that’s not counting every previous spouse or sexual partner. One of the major difficulties with relationships is that there are always two individuals, sometimes with two different agendas, each bringing their own emotional “baggage” into the mix. More often than not, this baggage is unconscious. Unknown. Out of awareness. These patterns can also sometimes be expressed within the therapy relationship itself. All this makes for a richly complex psychological stew. What is the secret to making sense of and constructively dealing with such frustrating, confusing, complicated, and oftentimes repetitive romantic relationship problems?

Let’s begin by taking a look at the pervasive problem of pathological or neurotic narcissism. Psychologically, narcissism—and it was Freud (1914) who first introduced this now ubiquitous term—is a neurotic self-absorption which, in effect, prevents someone from achieving true intimacy with another. What many people are not aware of is that neurotic narcissism is fundamentally informed by underlying narcissistic rage: an unrelenting need to repay any perceived slight or insult. Indeed, conversely, post-Freudian psychoanalysts like Winnicott, Fromm, Kohut, and Kernberg have attributed anger, rage, and hostility to an underlying matrix of neurotic narcissism. Neurotic narcissism starts out as normal narcissism, a healthy, natural childhood need for attention and appreciation which, when continually frustrated, becomes fixated and pathological. Neurotic narcissism stems from inadequate, insufficient, or traumatic parenting and resulting emotional injury, especially before 5 years of age, during what Freud called the pre-Oedipal stage of psychosexual development.

article continues after advertisement

Children at this tender age find any serious lack of attunement and attention—or certainly, any outright abuse, neglect, or emotional, if not physical, abandonment—an insult, a psychological injury, a traumatic psychic wound which distorts perceptions of themselves, the world, and their relationship to it. These can be, but are not necessarily, isolated traumatic events. More commonly, these traumas result from some daily deficiency or toxicity in the nature of the parenting and are referred to in the literature as narcissistic injuries or narcissistic wounding. Traumatic wounding during this delicate developmental phase is not fundamentally sexual, as Freud insisted. It’s more about a lack of love, acceptance, sensitivity, support, and caring on the part of one or both parents. Such insensitivity typically stems from some measure of pathological narcissism (or worse) in the parents.

When children experience parents or caretakers as unloving, rejecting, unresponsive, or hostile, they defensively react to this narcissistic wounding by creating a shell-like false self. This false self replaces, protects, and conceals the unaccepted, unloved, and damaged true self, while presenting a persona (Jung) based on what they perceive their parents and the world want them to be. A great deal of what pathological narcissism in adults disguises is unresolved infantile anger, resentment, and rage about not being recognized, accepted, and loved for who we are. This infantile anger or rage, along with feelings and beliefs of being unlovable and unworthy of love, is buried beneath the false self. It is repressed and dissociated, but not forgotten. Nor is it forgiven. Narcissistic rage from the past tends to be re-stimulated by intimate relationships in the present. In romantic relationships, which require emotional vulnerability and intimacy, feelings are inevitably re-injured, and the childhood rage resurfaces, with a vengeance. This is why I contend in my book, Anger, Madness, and the Daimonic (1996), that intimacy is “the provocateur par excellence of the daimonic,” referring to the repressed anger or rage triggered by the vulnerability of romantic relationships.

Freud’s original theory of narcissism derives, of course, from the famous Greek myth of Narcissus. Echo, a sweet and lovely nymph, falls madly in love at first sight with the impossibly attractive youth, Narcissus, only to have her hesitant overtures rudely rejected by him. Poor Echo is crushed and runs away, leaving nothing but her mellifluous disembodied voice to remember her by. But she’s totally enraged and embittered about her love being unreciprocated by the vain, egotistical, self-absorbed Narcissus, who is too busy admiring himself to notice her. As so often happens, her love turns to hate. So she appeals to Nemesis, the Greek god of revenge and retribution, to punish Narcissus for this humiliating rejection by causing him to suffer the same excruciating fate. This is not an unfamiliar sentiment when spurned by someone we love, much as we might wish to deny it. We can all relate to having had such hateful and vengeful feelings from time to time, if we are willing to be brutally honest with ourselves.

Sympathetic with Echo's painful plight, Nemesis answers her prayer. Soon after, Narcissus, spying his handsome reflection in a still pool of water, falls completely and utterly in love with his own mirrored image: obviously, an impossible, superficial, nonreciprocal, unilateral relationship. Unable to turn away for a moment from the fascinating reflection of his own beloved visage, even to obtain something to eat, Narcissus too eventually withers away and dies of starvation, leaving merely a lovely flower, now his namesake, in commemoration. Paradoxically, like the profoundly neurotic Narcissus, the narcissist starves for real love because he or she can never get enough in the present to compensate for the past. No amount of attention, affection, adoration, or adulation can satisfy the incessant craving for that which was never received in the distant past or can obviate the narcissist's profound feelings of inferiority, loneliness, and unlovability. So despite their considerable charm, affability, and attractiveness, narcissists feel empty, lonely, and unlovable inside but rigidly reject real love for fear of reliving the agony of losing it. Instead, they pursue only illusory, superficial, and ultimately emotionally unavailable partners such as themselves, and typically, those who serve to promote and perpetuate their grandiose self-image or persona and feed their insatiable appetite for constant "narcissistic supplies."
